sound: I rebuilt the profile from the saved records of all four baseline reports, and every line checks out against the record it cites. Glyman: co-CEO; Paribus 2014–2019, YC S15, acquired by Capital One 2016; Harvard BA in Economics and East Asian Studies, 2008–2012. Milton: Founder of Nikola, former CEO and Executive Chairman until 2020; dHybrid; St. George Security; UVU. Zhang: Melbourne CS 2004–2007. Ding: Columbia 2015, Expanse, Merge 2020; Credit Suisse shown only as a lead. No colleague or relative fact leaked. Audit fixes for Goldman/Google/Bloomberg colleagues, relative roles, Ford/Farley, Substack links and the Stefanie Gordon bio all hold. The temporary test file is deleted.

findings.title: 'He/She' after another person is credited to the subject on own pages, bio records and the subject's Wikipedia article
findings.evidence: buildProfile, wikipedia record 'Elizabeth Holmes': 'In 2009, Holmes hired Ramesh "Sunny" Balwani as president... He had previously worked at Lotus Development and Microsoft. He earned an MBA from the University of California, Berkeley.' gives Holmes roles Lotus Development and Microsoft plus a Berkeley MBA. An own-page or bio record with Stefanie Gordon's real ramp.com bio gives Glyman iQuanti, U. Delaware and an NYU MA.
findings.scenario: opensOnSubject returns true for any sentence that opens on She/He/They. buildProfile calls it for firstNamed (any own page, change or bio record) and for surnamed (the subject's Wikipedia article) without checking carry. So the pronoun after 'hired Balwani' or 'Stefanie Gordon is...' counts as the subject, and the reset in bringsInSomeoneElse is skipped. The same path sets `theirs` at line 724.
findings.fix: Do what profileModel.sentencesAboutThem does. Work out `pronoun` first, set firstNamed and surnamed only when !pronoun, and accept a pronoun sentence only through `follows` (carry > 0). In `theirs`, use opensOnSubject only for sentences that are not pronoun sentences, or are pronoun sentences with follows true. Add the Holmes/Balwani and Stefanie Gordon texts as negative tests.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. In the subject's Wikipedia article, the Holmes/Balwani text gives Holmes roles at Lotus Development and Microsoft plus a Berkeley MBA. A bio record and an own page about Stefanie Gordon both give Glyman an iQuanti role. opensOnSubject (line 169) returns true for any sentence that opens on He/She/They, so firstNamed, surnamed and theirs skip the reset in bringsInSomeoneElse.
findings.betterFix: Remove the pronoun branch from opensOnSubject. Accept a pronoun sentence only through `follows`, where carry > 0 and was reset by bringsInSomeoneElse. Compute theirs for a pronoun sentence as `follows`. Check that bioSentences and profileModel.sentencesAboutThem agree. Add the Holmes and Gordon texts as negative tests.

findings.title: Another person's title at the company becomes the subject's headline (e.g. 'Nikola CEO Mark Russell and founder Trevor Milton' makes Milton current CEO)
findings.evidence: buildProfile on one sentence each: 'Ramp CTO Karim Atiyeh and Eric Glyman spoke.' gives the headline 'CTO, Ramp'. 'Nikola CEO Mark Russell and founder Trevor Milton spoke in 2019.' gives 'CEO, Nikola', current. 'Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh, CTO of Ramp, spoke.' gives 'CTO, Ramp'. 'Trevor Milton, Nikola founder, was sued by Nikola CEO Steve Girsky.' gives 'Founder and CEO'.
findings.scenario: Pattern b ('<Company> TITLE') is accepted whenever the sentence names the subject and the text before the match is empty, even when another person's name follows the title directly. Pattern a takes 'Name and Other, CTO of Ramp' as a joint subject. For a person with no dated end record, the colleague's title becomes the headline and the current role.
findings.fix: Pattern b: when a person name (NAME_RUN with isPersonRun) that is not the subject follows the title within 3 characters, skip the match. Pattern a: accept it only when the subject's mention (•) sits directly before the title, as in '• , TITLE of Co' or '• (TITLE'. Never apply the joint-subject exemption to an appositive title. Add these four sentences as tests.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced all four sentences. The headlines come out as 'CTO, Ramp' (twice), 'CEO, Nikola' (current) and 'Founder and CEO, Nikola'. Pattern b accepts the match when nothing precedes it and the sentence names the subject, even when another person's name follows the title. Pattern a has no check after the match.
findings.betterFix: Pattern b: own the title only when the subject's name is directly after it (nameNext). If a person NAME_RUN that is not the subject follows within 3 characters, reject it. Pattern a: require the masked subject (•) directly before the title, with only ',', '(' or 'is/was/as the' in between. Treat '• and X, TITLE' as X's title.

findings.title: The model merge brings back an ended role as current and adds duplicate rows (Milton shown as current Nikola CEO)
findings.evidence: verifyProfile on a confirmed 2019 record 'Trevor Milton is the founder and CEO of Nikola...', then mergeProfile with a base role Nikola 'Founder, CEO, Executive Chairman' 2014–2020 current:false. Result: roles[0] = {org:'Nikola', title:'CEO', current:true} above the ended row. Education ends up with both 'Harvard College' and 'Harvard University'.
findings.scenario: verifyProfile sets current from the wording of a single quote ('is', 'oversees'), so an old article reads as current. mergeProfile keys roles on org+title and folds rows only when one has no title, so the model's 'Nikola CEO, current' sits on top of the pattern row that knows the role ended. Education is keyed on orgKey, while profile.js groups schools by rootOf.
findings.fix: In mergeProfile, when the base has a role at the same orgKey with current false (or with a to year), set the model row's current to false unless its record is dated after that end. Fold rows at the same organisation into one with joined titles. Group education with the same rootOf rule as profile.js (Harvard, Harvard College and Harvard University become one row).
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. A verified 'Nikola CEO, current:true' row sits above the base row 'Founder, CEO, Executive Chairman' 2014–2020 current:false. Harvard College and Harvard University stay as two rows. With no base headline, the headline becomes 'CEO, Nikola'. The current flag comes from 'is' in one undated quote.
findings.betterFix: In mergeProfile, after keying roles, compare every row at the same orgKey. If any row has a `to` year or current:false, set the model row's current to false unless its record date is later than that end. Fold rows at the same org into one row with the titles joined. Use profile.js rootOf for the education key.

findings.title: Funding, valuation and investors of another company in a sentence that only names the company are credited to the company
findings.evidence: buildCompanyFacts(Glyman/Ramp, confirmed record) on "Ramp's rival Brex, valued at $12 billion in 2022, raised $300 million in a Series D led by Greenoaks." gives Ramp a $12B valuation, a Series D and investor Greenoaks. The real r9 Zhang sentence about Alta, written with '$80 million', gives Airwallex an $80M round from Index Ventures, GV, Blackbird and Square Peg.
findings.scenario: namesCompany only checks that the company's name appears somewhere in the sentence. Every money figure in that sentence is then read as the company's round, valuation or revenue. Records comparing competitors ('Ramp vs Brex') or announcing the founder's new startup (Zhang's Alta, in r9) are common.
findings.fix: For each figure, find the organisation the clause is about: the nearest capitalised org name before the RAISE verb or 'valued at' within the clause. Keep the figure only when that org is a company form, or when the clause names no other org. Skip clauses with 'rival|competitor|new startup|which has raised' where another org is named. Add the Brex and Alta sentences as tests.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. The Brex sentence gives Ramp a $12B valuation, a $300M Series D and investor Greenoaks. namesCompany only checks that the company's name appears somewhere in the sentence. After that, every figure in the sentence is credited to the company.
findings.betterFix: For each figure, find the nearest capitalised organisation before the raise verb or 'valued at' in the same clause. Keep the figure only when that organisation is the company form, or when no other organisation is named in the clause. Words like 'rival', 'competitor' or 'new startup' before another org mean the clause is about that org. Add the Brex and Alta sentences as tests.

findings.title: 'worked at X for 2 years' loses the employer or reads it as 'Lazard for 3'
findings.evidence: 'Shensi Ding worked at Credit Suisse for 2 years before founding Merge.' gives no role. 'Eric Glyman previously worked at Lazard for 3 years.' gives the role 'Lazard for 3'. A Wikipedia sentence gave both 'Worthington Industries for 20' and '20'.
findings.scenario: In the second rolePattern, the optional filler group `(?:[\p{L}\s'’-]{0,40}?\s)?` is tried before it is skipped, so it absorbs 'at Credit Suisse ' and the match ends at 'for '. The org read there is '2' (dropped) or a lower-case word (no org), so the true employer is lost. Separately, ORG_JOIN accepts 'for' followed by a digit token, which gives 'Lazard for 3'. This is one of the most common ways a career is written.
findings.fix: Stop the filler group from crossing at/for: use `(?:(?!\b(?:at|for)\b)[\p{L}\s'’-]){0,40}?`. In ORG_RE, do not join across 'for' or 'of' when the next token is a digit or lower case. Reject purely numeric orgs in okOrg. Add tests: 'for 2 years', 'for two years', 'for three years as an analyst'.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. 'worked at Credit Suisse for 2 years' gives no role, and 'previously worked at Lazard for 3 years' gives the org 'Lazard for 3'. The proposed causes (the lazy filler group and ORG_JOIN joining across 'for' and a digit) match the code.
findings.betterFix: As proposed. Also strip a trailing ' (for|of) <number>' in trimOrg, and reject orgs that are purely numeric or end in a number word.

findings.title: The 'someone else' guard drops true facts after 'with <co-founder>' or 'told <publisher>'
findings.evidence: 'Eric Glyman, who co-founded Ramp with Karim Atiyeh, graduated from Harvard University in 2012.' gives no education. 'Eric Glyman co-founded Paribus with Karim Atiyeh and later joined Capital One.' gives no Capital One. 'Shensi Ding, who started Merge with Gil Feig, previously worked at Expanse.' gives no Expanse. 'Eric Glyman told Bloomberg he previously worked at Lazard.' gives nothing.
findings.scenario: OTHER_LEAD fires on 'with', 'told' and similar words followed by any capital letter, anywhere between the subject and the claim. A co-founder clause (very common in founder bios) or a publisher name therefore removes every later claim in the sentence. This thins the profile, which was the owner's second complaint.
findings.fix: Count OTHER_LEAD only when the word after it starts a NAME_RUN that isPersonRun (Bloomberg is not one), and only when the claim is inside that person's own clause: the name is followed by ', who/a/an/the/former' or by a verb of its own. Reset the guard at a closing ', ' of a relative clause or at 'and (later|then)?' + verb, which returns to the main subject.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced all four sentences: each loses its Harvard, Capital One, Expanse or Lazard fact. OTHER_LEAD fires on 'with' or 'told' followed by any capital letter, anywhere after the subject. Any fix must keep the existing negative tests passing, such as the Karim Atiyeh 'who previously worked at Goldman' case.
findings.betterFix: Keep OTHER_LEAD, but require the word after it to start a person NAME_RUN (isPersonRun). Reset the segment at the end of the other person's clause: the closing ', ' of a relative clause, or ' and (later|then)? <verb>'. The guard then still blocks 'with Karim Atiyeh, who previously worked at X'. Run the founderR3.profile colleague tests as the regression check.

findings.title: Any sentence naming a 'Business School' or 'College' becomes education (talks, donations, board seats)
findings.evidence: 'Eric Glyman spoke at Columbia Business School in 2023.' gives education Columbia Business School. Same for 'gave the commencement address at Babson College', 'donated to Stanford University to fund a school of engineering', and 'sits on the board of Harvard Business School Club' (Harvard Business School).
findings.scenario: EDU_WORD includes bare 'school', 'college' and 'education', so the school's own name satisfies the check. Then SCHOOL takes any school in a sentence that opens on the person. An investor reads a degree the person never earned.
findings.fix: Test EDU_WORD on the sentence with the SCHOOL matches blanked out. Drop bare school/college/education from the trigger. Require an education verb or degree (graduated, studied, attended, enrolled, earned/received a degree, alum, class of, 'NN, dropped out) in the clause before or right after the school. Never take a school that follows 'spoke at', 'board of', 'donated to' or 'lecture at'.
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. Columbia Business School (from a talk), Babson College (from a commencement address) and Harvard Business School (from a board seat at its club) all become education. EDU_WORD matches 'school' and 'college' inside the school's own name.
findings.betterFix: Test EDU_WORD on the sentence with the SCHOOL matches blanked out, and drop bare school, college and education from the trigger. Skip a school directly after 'spoke at', 'address at', 'board of', 'donated to' or 'lecture at', or one followed by 'Club'.

findings.title: 'Left without a degree' and the YC batch are computed but never shown, so a dropout reads as an alumnus
findings.evidence: buildProfile on Milton's real Wikipedia record gives Utah Valley University with note 'left without a degree'. Resume.js line 86 renders only degree and field, and line 96 renders only with and outcome. grep finds no use of `note` or `program` in Resume.js or reportText.js. mergeProfile's education fill list leaves out note.
findings.scenario: The ground truth for Milton (UVU, no degree) and Holmes (Stanford, left 2004) asks for these items. The card shows only 'Utah Valley University', which reads as a degree. Paribus's 'Y Combinator S15' is dropped in the same way.
findings.fix: Render e.note in the education Line detail (for example 'left without a degree') and x.program in the founded detail, in Resume.js and in reportText.js. Add 'note' to the education fill list in profileModel.mergeProfile so the model merge keeps it.
findings.verifyNote: buildProfile sets note 'left without a degree' for Utah Valley University (verified) and sets program for YC. Resume.js renders only degree and field for education, and only with and outcome for founded. mergeProfile's education fill list leaves out note, and its founded fill list leaves out program.
findings.betterFix: Render e.note in the education detail and x.program in the founded detail, in Resume.js and in the report's text output. Add 'note' to the education fill list and 'program' to the founded fill list in mergeProfile.

findings.title: A degree after the year is missed, and a sentence-final period stays on the school name
findings.evidence: 'Eric Glyman graduated from Harvard in 2012 with a BA in Economics.' gives Harvard, to 2012, degree null and field null. '...an MBA from the University of California, Berkeley.' gives the school 'University of California, Berkeley.' with the period.
findings.scenario: schoolDetails reads 'with a BA' only directly after the school, so the common '<school> in 2012 with a BA in X' word order loses the degree and the field. SCHOOL_SRC tokens accept '.', so a sentence-final period becomes part of the name and breaks rootOf grouping.
findings.fix: Let the after-match accept an optional `(?:in\s+(?:19|20)\d\d\s+)?` before `(?:with|,)`, and take the year from it. Trim a trailing '.' from SCHOOL matches unless it ends an abbreviation (St., Jr.).
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. 'graduated from Harvard in 2012 with a BA in Economics' gives degree null and field null. 'University of California, Berkeley.' keeps the sentence-final period, which also splits rootOf grouping.
findings.betterFix: As proposed. Allow an optional 'in YYYY' before 'with' in the after-regex. Trim a trailing period from SCHOOL matches unless the last token is a known abbreviation.

findings.title: 'launched a new blockchain startup, Alta' is not read as a venture (Zhang's current company missing)
findings.evidence: The real r9 record news-archive-n4csl9 says 'Airwallex co-founder and CEO Jack Zhang has launched a new blockchain infrastructure startup, Alta, which has raised...'. buildProfile gives founded only Airwallex. 'Jack Zhang launched Alta in 2026.' gives Alta.
findings.scenario: foundedRe accepts only a capitalised name or 'a ... startup called/named X' after the verb. The appositive '<a ... startup>, X,' is the usual press wording, so the founder's newest venture is left out of the résumé.
findings.fix: In the founded pattern's lead-in, also accept `(?:an?|the|her|his|their)\s+(?:[\p{L}-]+\s+){0,5}?(?:company|startup|start-up|venture|firm|fund),\s+` followed by the org, with the same mine() guard. Mirror the change in extract.companiesFromText (its 'a startup, X' form exists only for marketplace/company/startup directly after the article).
findings.verifyNote: Reproduced. In 'has launched a new blockchain infrastructure startup, Alta, ...' the founded list gives only Airwallex. The foundedRe lead-in requires 'called' or 'named' after the noun.
findings.betterFix: Accept '<article> ... (startup|company|venture|firm|fund),\s+' in the lead-in, in both foundedRe and ORG_LEAD, under the same mine() guard. Mirror the change in extract.companiesFromText.
